parakeet: The love I had for my children demanded more for me than faith could ever offer. So when people ask me about the secret catalyst for my deconversion, I always come back here. It wasn't some book or debate or late night crisis. It was the weight of being a father. The love I had for my children demanded more for me than faith could ever offer. It pushed me toward honesty. It pushed me toward freedom, and it pushed me out of religion for them, but also for me. When people ask me what made me leave the faith, they usually expect me to name a book I read, a debate I watched, or some single moment where it all fell apart. But that's not my story. My deconversion wasn't sparked by one dramatic revelation. It wasn't a lightning strike. It was slower, quieter, and in some ways much heavier. The secret catalyst for me was fatherhood. Becoming a parent magnified every crack in the foundation of my theology. Each time I sat in a hospital room, watching my children delivered by C-section, I was reminded of just how fragile life is. Those moments didn't feel like divine providence. They felt like survival, depending on human knowledge and human hands. They exposed how flimsy God's plan sounded when what really stood between life and death was a scapel and a surgeon. Every conversation I had with my son pulled me further from the easy answers I had grown up on. His questions tested the integrity of my beliefs, and in his eyes, I could see what I always wanted as a child. Someone to take me seriously, to be honest with me, to let me wrestle with the hard questions instead of silencing me with faith. If I wanted that for him, I had to live it for myself. Every reflection on purpose forced me to face a choice. I could raise my kids the way I was raised, telling them their futures were already written and that their lives were about fulfilling someone else's plan. Or I could parent with intention, showing them that meaning isn't handed down from the sky. It's built through the choices we make, the love we give, and the honesty we practice. And every time I leaned into honesty, choosing not to indoctrinate, choosing not to repeat what I no longer believed, I felt myself pulled further from the comfort of religion. It was as if fatherhood demanded a higher standard of truth than faith could really provide. In the end, my children didn't just make me a parent. They made me a seeker of truth. They made me a challenger of old assumptions. They made me someone who could no longer stay in the faith. Not because I wanted to tear it all down, but because love required me to build something better.
